messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Multi_normal wants positive defined covariance matrix - while mine is NOT
parts:
On Wednesday, June 8, 2016 at 1:43:27 AM UTC-4, Stefano wrote:
My knowledge in statistics is not enough to understand why a positively and neg correlated matrix is not suitable for multi_norm sampling. Unless the non-positiveness is related to some other property of my data.
And why a positively defined matrix is required for multi_normal sampling?

It isn't related to any other property of the data. One definition of a positive definite covariance matrix is one that has all positive eigenvalues. You covariance matrix has 6 positive eigenvalues and 500 that are zero. This implies that if you knew any 6 genes for a person, you could figure out the other 500 with certainty. Does that seem reasonable?

The problem is that the maximum likelihood estimator of a covariance matrix is not very good unless the number of rows is large relative to the number of columns, whereas the opposite is true in your case once you transpose the matrix. You should look into shrunken covariance matrix estimators that do not suffer from this problem before attempting to use multi_normal in Stan.

Ben

parts:
Reading about shrinkage covariance estimation for matrices when "the sample size n is small and the number of considered variables p is large" I came across a solution that I adopted already "the diagonal matrix containing sample variances on the diagonal and zeros everywhere else". [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimation_of_covariance_matrices]

In asking whether this is a meaningful solution for me, I briefly introduce my problem. I will limit the description to the part here this problem arises, so sorry if it's not as clear as it could be.

In a mixture model

PRODUCT_sample ( PRODUCT_cellType ( PRODUCT_gene (               proportion_cellType_sample ~ dir()    *     expression_gene_cell_type                 )  )  )

having SUM_genes (expression_cell_type) = 1

for expression_gene_cell_type  I could use:

1) a given number being the mean gene expression for cell_type; soft_max transformed
2) a parameter with prior dirichlet(..) with hyperparameter proportional to mean gene expression for cell_type
3) a parameter with prior multi_normal( .. , ..) soft_max transformed

The latter case (3) gives me opportunity to use the variance (of gene expression) information as well.

The question is: in the case I cannot estimate the covariances because the number of samples is small; would it make sense to assume all covariances are 0 (genes independent) and use the variances as diagonal?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Multi_normal wants positive defined covariance matrix - while mine is NOT
parts:
> On Jun 8, 2016, at 4:12 AM, Stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ... I could use:

>
> 1) a given number being the mean gene expression for cell_type; soft_max transformed
> 2) a parameter with prior dirichlet(..) with hyperparameter proportional to mean gene expression for cell_type
> 3) a parameter with prior multi_normal( .. , ..) soft_max transformed
>
> The latter case (3) gives me opportunity to use the variance (of gene expression) information as well.
>
> The question is: in the case I cannot estimate the covariances because the number of samples is small; would it make sense to assume all covariances are 0 (genes independent) and use the variances as diagonal?

Case (3) is more flexible as a prior, but if you don't have
enough data to estimate the covariance, you have to fall back
to a diagonal or use a strong prior (the latter being a generic
escape for non-identifiability in a Bayesian model). In which
case, you'll probably be close to case (2).

- Bob
